newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Ifo sees stronger European growth in '97.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Ifo sees stronger European growth in '97.

text.p: Western Europe's economy will extend its moderate upturn in 1997, with growth averaging 2-1/4 percent compared to 1.5 percent last year, Germany's Ifo institute said in a forecast on Thursday.
Monetary policy will be expansive, but that will be offset by fiscal belt-tightening as governments try to rein in borrowing to qualify for the single European currency.
Export and capital investment will show the strongest growth rates, and industry will increase stocks. But building and state consumption will barely grow, Munich-based Ifo said.
Private consumption will grow at the same rate as in 1996, and inflationary pressures will remain subdued, with consumer prices on average rising by around two percent.
But the stronger growth will have little impact on the jobs market, with unemployment rates remaining high at an average 10.5 percent.
Ifo gave the following country comments:

FRANCE -- After choppy economic developments and industrial unrest, a moderate upturn can be expected this year with growth of around two percent. Expansion will be export-led and helped by monetary easing in 1995 and 1996.

BRITAIN -- Economic expansion will remain lively but slow in the second half of the year, with growth forecast at three percent in 1997. Monetary policy is still expansive, and retail prices will grow faster than elsewhere in western Europe.

ITALY -- Production and demand will barely pick up in 1997, with fiscal tightening and high real interest rates keeping growth unchanged at one percent. A rise in the lira rate will dampen exports. Policy will stay focused on EMU qualification.

SPAIN -- Economic growth will accelerate to 2.5 percent, helped by monetary stimulus, a stronger world economy and supply-side policies. But the high peseta exchange rate is no longer a boost to exports. Unemployment to stay high.
NETHERLANDS -- Recovery to continue into 1997, with growth remaining at 2.5 percent without tensions building in economy.

SWITZERLAND -- Stagnation stretching back to 1991 will turn into a modest upturn around mid-year. Low interest rates and pickup in Europe will be offset by tight fiscal policy, the high franc exchange rate and structural impediments.
BELGIUM -- Capital investment and exports will help growth accelerate to two percent in 1997. Wage moderation and dollar strength to help stabilise the economy.
AUSTRIA -- Slack domestic demand will be offset by stronger exports, but growth to remain modest at 1.5 percent in 1997.
SWEDEN -- Economy to remain buoyant despite budget consolidation efforts. 1997 growth forecast at 2.5 percent.
DENMARK -- Recovery which began in 1996 will continue this year at a slightly faster pace of 2.5 percent.
NORWAY -- Economic performance will remain strong despite wage round seen hitting export competitiveness. Growth to slow to 3.5 percent in 1997 from five percent in 1996.
FINLAND -- Growth of three percent expected this year despite fiscal consolidation, led by investment and exports.
